title: Lead removal of infrastructure, visa and safety deficits

blocks.text: Theme 3.2 · Governance and leadership · Focus area 19
Lead removal of infrastructure, visa and safety deficits

Visas, air rights, the runway and policing sit with national government, so the province leads by escalation backed with evidence, and delivers the safety programmes and basic services that are its own.

Visas, air rights, airport capacity and policing shape how many visitors reach the province and how safe they feel. The province holds few of these levers. National government holds visa rules, border compliance and air service agreements. The province holds safety programmes and local government holds basic services (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p58). ACSA, a national body, holds the runway (section 2.4). Escalation is therefore the province's main tool for the national share.

The deficits bear hardest on the markets the growth case needs. Chinese and Middle Eastern travellers face slow, document-heavy visa processes (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p51). The Table Mountain Aerial Cableway cites visas as a constraint on growth from India and recovery from China, and the CTICC on regional African events (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p36, p45).

Inside the province, safety and basic services gate both visits and community growth. Nine of the 20 shortlisted communities record a safety-perception gap and five record extortion. A formal safety assessment remains a separate requirement before any community product launches (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p30, p35). Two provincial documents and the City's framework name safety as a constraint, and the City's stakeholders rank it the first priority for growth (City of Cape Town, Tourism Development Framework 2019 to 2024, p4; Tourism Blueprint 2030, p4; Provincial Economic Review and Outlook 2025, p4). The road from the airport is one concern. The Department of Mobility's draft framework flags the N2 from Cape Town International as a congestion and safety problem for tourists (Western Cape Department of Mobility, draft Provincial Land Transport Framework, Apr 2025, ch12). Congestion costs the Metro an estimated R2.8 billion a year, and water scarcity acts as a hard ceiling on visitor load in high-growth nodes (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p38). Here the province and the municipalities hold part of the answer.

blocks.message: Ten of the 16 organisations raise the deficits, and most of the levers sit with national government or SOEs.

blocks.text: Stakeholders raise the deficits widely. Ten of the 16 organisations raised them, and safety perception alone came from seven (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p20 to p46, counted). Yet even this evidence, broad as it is, is statement rather than measure. No visa processing time is in hand for any priority market (section 5.2). The nearest national measure is an outcome: in its first year the eVisa processed fewer than half its applications and rejected 93% of those it decided (BDO for DEDAT, Western Cape Visa Regime Study, Jul 2024, p12).

National reform can move arrivals. Ghanaian arrivals to South Africa reached 36,656 in 2024, a level the source credits to the visa waiver without printing an earlier year (Skift African Market Analysis, 16 Mar 2026, s4.6; arrivals to South Africa, not Cape Town) [Ghana visa waiver start date, given as 1 November 2023 and as 2024: Wesgro Research to confirm]. E-visa expansion and the Trusted Tour Operator Scheme are promising, but their effect on Western Cape arrivals is not yet proven (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p34). The province's task is to make the case for reform in its own markets, with its own numbers.

Wesgro runs a standing escalation agenda at Steerco. Each item names the decision, the national body that owns it and the date the province asks for. The first agenda is tabled in 2027 (section 4.3). It covers visa categories and processing for China, India, the Middle East and Africa. It also covers air service agreements and immigration throughput at Cape Town International. The visa asks start from DEDAT's visa regime study, which ranks published processing times first and visa exemption for China, India and Nigeria second (BDO for DEDAT, Western Cape Visa Regime Study, Jul 2024, p34). The agenda takes the reforms that bear on visitors and first checks what has moved since 2024. Wesgro's Advocacy and Advisory unit was set up to build evidence-based policy feedback on levers the province does not control (Wesgro, Strategic Plan 2025/26 to 2029/30, p27). Once Wesgro confirms its remit, the unit runs the agenda day to day. Research and Destination Marketing build the evidence for each ask, market by market. Stakeholder insights already point to the evidence needed: the safety issues most damaging to demand and the access barriers across air, visas and onward travel (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p14).

The province delivers its own share in parallel. The Metro needs dedicated tourism safety units and programmes (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p41). The City's framework for 2019 to 2024 proposed them. Its Tourist Safety Programme set out secure zones, a Tourist Police unit, victim support and safety forums (City of Cape Town, Tourism Development Framework 2019 to 2024, p5). From 2027 the City and the Western Cape Government, with the other municipalities and SAPS, build on whichever parts run, once the City confirms them (section 2.4). Safety compacts follow in pilot communities. Municipalities and CapeNature fix basic services, water and connectivity at remote reserves and in tourism towns. Wesgro carries a visitor-safety narrative in its marketing. It applies the four launch gates set in focus area 13 to any community product it sells. From 2029 responses to the national asks are logged and followed up each quarter.

blocks.text: Escalation works when the ask is specific and the evidence is local. The method has already moved decisions taken elsewhere. Cape Town added 17 mainline international routes from 2015 to 2025, more than any of eight secondary-airport peers, a record credited to Wesgro's commercial and relationship-driven route development (focus area 17). A standing agenda keeps each ask alive across budget cycles, so a refusal becomes a follow-up rather than an end. It also gives coordination one anchor. Chile's coordination is most powerful when anchored around a single strategic constraint, long-haul access (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p59). Action on its own share, from safety units to basic services, strengthens the province's hand when it asks others to act.

Chile shows what national access policy can achieve. It runs one of the world's most liberal aviation systems, using open-skies agreements, strong aviation institutions and private sector participation (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p23). Passenger traffic at Santiago's airport rose from about 16 million in 2010 to more than 26 million in 2019 (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p25, p26). For the Western Cape, the lesson is to lobby actively for air service liberalisation and simplified visa regimes (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p28). Kenya reduces entry friction to position Nairobi as a regional hub (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p59). No comparator shows a region escalating to its national government, so the province's own record is the first real test. The condition is a national answer. The province cannot compel one, so it measures what it can: visa processing times in priority markets and the share of its asks answered (section 5.2).
